utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Morning, ladies and gentlemen. Appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours please, my name is Grant Niemann, I appear with my colleagues Ms. McHenry, Mr. Turone and Mr. Khan for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Can we have the appearances for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours my name is Edina Residovic, Defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic, appearing together with my colleague Eugene O'Sullivan, professor from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Zeljko Olujic, appearing on behalf of Mr. Zdravko Mucic with my colleague, Michael Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Salih Karabdic, attorney from Sarajevo, defending, with Mr. Thomas Moran, attorney from Houston, Texas, Mr. Hazim Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, I am John Ackerman, I appear on behalf of Mr. Esad Landzo and with me as co-counsel is Ms. Cynthia McMurrey.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Before the witnesses is brought in, may I ask the court to cover one little matter? I think about two weeks ago Mr. Landzo had filed a motion for a hearing on a memorandum sent around by the Registry on October 15. I was wondering whether it would be possible for us to schedule some kind of hearing between now and November 6th at your convenience of course. I want to remind the court we were requesting a hearing on the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Discuss it with the legal officer and they will react appropriately. Can we have the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: While the witness is being brought in, may I ask for the court's permission to have an analyst and the translator present in the video booth for portions of the testimony, because later on I will be showing this witness some excerpts from video. I understand your Honours have to give permission for anyone other than court staff to be in the room. I believe we did this once before. If I could ask your Honour's permission to have an analyst and interpreter in the video booth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: As long they are not going to be witnesses in the case we have no objection to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: They could not be witnesses if they have already performed such a role.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: We agree, your Honour, with you. Our position is exactly yours, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. (Witness enters court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly remind the witness that he is still on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I am reminding you, sir, that you are still under oath. GENERAL JOVAN DIVJAK (continued)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning to you all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. I believe when we left yesterday you had just finished giving a brief explanation of your career; may I ask you now to describe briefly how the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was created, and how it developed between April and the beginning of December 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, I have to say that there was an aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina, which followed the aggression against Croatia, the aggression started by the Yugoslav People's Army, which was joined by paramilitary formations from Serbian Montenegro and paramilitary units of the SDS Party, the party of the Bosnian Serbs. When I say that the first aggression was by the Yugoslav People's Army, I corroborate this by the fact that virtually the entire armaments and military equipment that was in Croatia in 1991 after the agreement on a cessation of hostilities in Croatia reached by Milosevic and Tudjman on January 1st, 1992, units of the Yugoslav People's Army were deployed in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Bosnian Herzegovina at that time took steps to be recognised as a state, both by the European Community and the United Nations organisation. The run for Presidency of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia -- in the work of which for half a year representatives from Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatia Slovenia and Macedonia did not participate -- at the end of 1991 decided to engage the Yugoslav army to protect the rights of the Serbs in the same way that it had done previously in Croatia, so it now decided to do the same in Bosnia-Herzegovina. As for the arguments in support of this, I refer to the statements of the President of the Presidency of Yugoslavia at the time, Mr. Jovic, and the Chief of Staff of the Yugoslav People's Army at the time, who speak of the decisions to protect the Serbian people who are in jeopardy in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. When talking about the threats to the security of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I also wish to refer you to the first aggression committed against Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is in the village of Ravno, which belongs to the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The attack was carried out at the end of September, 1991, on the pretext that in the village of Ravno the Croatian army had been deployed and in their assessment the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina needed to be protected against attack by the Croatian army. There are documents to show that in September voluntary units or units of volunteers from Montenegro and Serbia and units of the Yugoslav People's Army from the Podgorica and Uzice Corps, with the enthusiastic support of the SDS Party and their followers in the area of Herzegovina, reached as far as Mostar by the end of the year. I apologise for going into these details, but I need to explain why, due to such relationships, the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina had to organise its defences and how it proceeded to do so. It is important for an understanding of the situation, to say that already at the end of 1990 and the beginning of 1991 from the depots of the Yugoslav People's Army, some members of the Serbian Democratic Party were armed by JNA barracks and trained there. When talking about these arguments, there are documents in our Institute for War Crimes dealing with these matters and which were captured by the second military district during the war. It is noteworthy that Bosnia and Herzegovina accepted its authorities and its Presidency while the members of that Presidency and those authorities representing the Serb people obstructed its work. Already in November they set up parallel authorities to the legal authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina. They formed their own Assembly in February 1992. They passed their own constitution and they sought to impose their own authority. At first in the municipalities in which the Serbs constituted a majority, and as of September with the actual supports of units of the JNA, they established their authority in places where they were not in a majority, such as was the case in Foca, Visegrad, Zvornik. Mostly in all settlements bordering on the territory of Serbia and Montenegro. At the end of 1991 and the beginning of 1992, with the support of tanks and artillery from the barracks in Sarajevo, they withdrew and established positions that overlooked the city and that dominated the city. The armoured and mechanised units of the Yugoslav People's Army were deployed in areas where they never were stationed before. These were strategic directions of action which lead from Croatia and Serbia towards Sarajevo. In view of such a situation, the political leadership of Bosnia-Herzegovina continued to seek peaceful ways to achieve -- there was some discussion over a federation and in these negotiations a prominent role was played by the Izetbegovic and the President of Macedonia. However, in view of the fact, and there is evidence of this too, that the plan to create a greater Serbia, which applied to the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, has been in existence for at least 200 years and this was an opportunity for extremist forces in both Serbia and among the Bosnian Serbs to fulfil that aim. On 6th April, 1992, the European Union accepted or recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina as a state within its historical boundaries. It accepted the organisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina as it was set up at the time, with the structure that was formed at the 1990 elections. On that day, the 6th April, Bosnia acquired statehood but it did not have armed forces to defend what Europe had recognised -- that is, its statehood. May I make a brief digression? In Yugoslavia there were two organised armed forces. There were the armed forces within the Yugoslav People's Army, and there was the Territorial Defence. The Yugoslav People's Army had as its duty to protect the constitutional system and territorial integrity of Yugoslavia. Each Republic organised its Territorial Defence, the main aim being to combat what was then known as the internal and external enemy, or rather it was a force which in situations, in crisis situations, was to ensure, for Yugoslavia and for Bosnian Herzegovina, stability. According to the constitution of Yugoslavia, the Republics were in command of the Territorial Defence. However, in 1990, the Presidency passed a decision to withdraw weapons and material from companies and other state-run institutions, and to put them in the Territorial Defence warehouses, and to support my claim that the plan on the aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina was not made in 24 hours but that it took longer, I offer the fact that on 8th May 1991 the Presidency of Yugoslavia -- again, I must say that it was a rump Presidency, because four Republics were not represented in it -- passed the decision for the entire equipment of the Territorial Defence should be stationed in the Territorial Defence warehouses. This was a way for the JNA to exclude the possibility of the Republics defending their territorial integrity. So, on 6th April, without their own army, and with the Territorial Defence, which was without arms and ammunition, the Presidency in such a traumatic situation decided that the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina should be formed, the main aim being to defend the territorial integrity and the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina where for thousands of years Serbs, Bosniaks, Croats, Jews and Romanies had lived. We in Bosnia-Herzegovina had a locality known as Prnjavor, where 24 different ethnic groups were represented. On 6th April, when the decision was taken, the TO staff of Bosnia-Herzegovina was formed. I recall that I said yesterday that the main aim of the Presidency was the staff to reflect the percentage share of the population in terms of ethnicity who at that moment were in favour of the idea contained in the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina. When the TO staff was formed, it sent to its subordinate staffs or, to be more precise, every municipality in Bosnian Herzegovina had its own TO headquarters. We asked the municipal staffs to state whether they supported the newly formed TO staff. All those staffs in which the Serbs were not in the majority confirmed in writing their support and sent lists of names of people who endorsed the staff of Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina and who supported the decision of the Presidency to set up that Republic's TO. Out of the 109 municipalities prior to the aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina, 73 municipal staffs signed and expressed their support for the Presidency and the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina being the institution that enjoyed their support. Parallel with the formation of the municipal staffs, groups of patriotic citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina were formed. The best organised and most numerous was the Patriotic League. Then, side by side with them, were the groups known as the Green Berets and the police of Bosnia-Herzegovina was fully committed, and I must give an explanation; namely, the Serbs who were members of the joint police force abandoned it when the parallel authorities were set up by the Bosnian Serbs, so that in the police stations only members of the Bosniak and Croatian peoples remained. As in the case of the TO at the beginning and later in the BiH army, a number of Serbs stayed with the police and the army. On 15th April, 1992, the Presidency passed the decision according to which all these combat groups patriotic groups had to come under the umbrella of the Territorial Defence, so as to combine the activities of all units within the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In May the Presidency passed the decision to set up the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. At the same time a law on defence was adopted, according to which in the course of the war the armed forces were formed which were to comprise the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Croatian Defence Council, the police, units of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, that is the police, and armed formations of enterprises or companies that had their own units. Briefly, with reference to the HVO, I must point out that politically among the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina there were extremists and towards the end of 1991 the desire was expressed for the Croats to finally, after a thousand years, should have a chance to form their own state. There are documents in which the leaders of the HDZ at the time expressed their wishes and aspirations. You will probably be discussing one such political statement with one of the people who will be present at future hearings. Rather like the Serbs, they formed their own parallel authorities. They formed the Croatian Community of Herceg Bosna and units of the Croatian Defence Council. The law on defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina stipulates that the HVO is part of the armed forces; however, regrettably, with the exception of HVO units in Sarajevo and in the Posavina region those units later implemented the policies of the HDZ, which was not in accordance with the law on defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask you, with respect to the HVO, in 1992 in particular, April to December of 1992, even if officially they were supposed to be under the authority of the municipal headquarters, do you know whether or not in fact they were often under the authority of the municipal headquarters, in fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They were under the authority of the municipal headquarters, but in the Croatian Community of Herceg Bosna, that is in the settlements and the municipalities where the Croatians, the Croatian community, they were under the authority of the Croatian community. But those who were in Posavina, first they were under the command of the Territorial Defence and later under the command of the army of Bosnian Herzegovina. It is important to make a comparison here. Just as the Serbian people in Bosnia formed their own authority and their own military units, in the similar way the Croatian extremists formed their own authorities and military units.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did I understand you -- do I understand your answer, sir, then, to mean that in the period of 1992 there were some areas where the HVO did not act under the authorities of the municipal headquarters, even if officially on paper they were supposed to. Is that what you are saying, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I repeat, they were under the command of the municipal headquarters where the majority of the population was Bosniak, and where they were -- they worked together with the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, they were part of the units of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and not under the command of the municipal headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did I then understand you that in some areas the HVO did act in fact under the authority of the municipal headquarters, and in other areas where the Bosnian Muslims were not in the majority they did not necessarily act under the authority of the municipal headquarters, is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first part is correct, the second is not, because where the Bosnians were in majority they formed part, together with the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There were -- they all had an equal status and formed mixed units, or were under the command of the Supreme Commander within that area, that is in a municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let me go back a minute, sir. You indicated that some time in May in Sarajevo there was, the law was changed to create the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Could you, please, just explain a little more, in fact, how the TO was transformed into the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, including whether or not it all happened in May, immediately upon the law being passed or did it take some amount of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Taking into account that the Territorial Defence was at first conceived to continue with the tasks and duties that it had originally, due to the threat to Bosnia-Herzegovina throughout its territory, and with unification of all groups in mind, a decision was adopted to establish the army of Bosnian Herzegovina as a new way of defending Bosnia-Herzegovina. In this way the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina got a strong command structure and the relation, the clear relationship of seniority was established. The army became a much more coherent force than was the Territorial Defence. At first, the Brigades were established.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, when were the Brigades established, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depended on different parts. One of the first Brigades, and there is a little bit of rivalry there in Bosnia-Herzegovina, are -- the first one was formed in late May and early June in Zenica. Those who were organising the defence in Tuzla also claimed that they formed their own around this same time, and by September the Corps were already established. The establishment of the army was made possible because certain amount of arms and ammunition was procured and the question may be asked, in what manner? Our weapons were in the depots of the JNA. The President of Bosnia-Herzegovina demanded that the arms that belonged to the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina be returned to the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it was not done. A part of the weaponry in the JNA depots was blocked by the TO and so the Territorial Defence armed itself. Later, during the combat operations in Bosnia-Herzegovina in May through July, part of the weaponry and ammunition was captured from the aggressor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, is it the case that when the TO was being transformed into the Bosnian army that there was a name change, that so instead of the TO within a municipality it became the municipal headquarters of the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The structure was changed so that at first the municipal headquarters, which had maybe larger authority than after the army was formed, was renamed into the army headquarters, because it was supposed to unify the police and the HVO and the Territorial Defence and the army units. However, since this was not functioning in a satisfactory manner at the level of the municipal headquarters, their role was diminished and after the Brigades were established, and especially after the Corps were established, their duties were reduced to practically two; first, to work on the mobilisations, and second, to provide logistical support for the units that had been formed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, who had the authority to appoint the TO Commanders, both in the beginning, in the very beginning of the war, and then as the TO was changed into the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the level of the municipal headquarters, at the Republic headquarters, it was the Presidency who had the authority. Often it happened that on behalf of the Presidencies, and this is dependent on the situation on the ground, the Chief of Staff of the Territorial Defence, and later the Bosnian army had the authority to sign appointments. Later the municipal headquarters would propose appointments and the Chief of Staff would sign them or approve them. Later, after the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was established, part of the authority to appoint the command staff was transferred to the Corps commands, and the Brigade commands.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, in the beginning, to whom were the TO Commanders responsible, particularly in areas where regional headquarters did not exist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were directly responsible to the main headquarters or the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In other words, there was a direct link, chain, between the main headquarters and the subordinate headquarters in the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And when you say "the main headquarters", you mean the main headquarters in Sarajevo, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in Sarajevo. And it would be the Commander and his deputies. Within the structure there is a chain of command, and there are deputies, depending whether there was sort of logistics, communications, political officer and the things like that, and they were a subordinate.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were there military police that were part of the TO and then later on part of the municipal headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is going further into the details of the organisation of the formations. One is to bear in mind that within the municipal headquarters and that first in the Republic headquarters there was a body which had the task to protect the units and individuals and facilities from the enemy operations and that was called the security body. It formed its own commands for protection of documents, facilities, and in principle all the units, from the municipal headquarters up to the Brigades, established their own police. For instance, in May 1992 we established a battalion of the military police, which was part of the Republican headquarters of the Territorial Defence, and its main duty was to protect the facilities and persons who were in top positions of authority within the headquarters. Such a body was supposed to be formed at the level of the municipal headquarters and the police was supposed to be involved in those duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, you have mentioned before the problems on the ground. Let me ask you: during the beginning period, after the war started, were there sometimes problems in following the proper procedure according to the law or according to official orders because of, among other things, problems on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One is to look at the situation comprehensively to understand fully the organisation of the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. On the one hand, there were laws and regulations, which in that period, in my view, did regulate the system of, and the chain of command rather well. However, predominantly based on objective reasons, sometimes even subjective, this system was unable to function, and I will point to an example; for instance, we said that in the law on defence the defence forces are comprised of the army, the HVO, the police and the armed groups that were supposed to protect, save facilities. However, rarely was that implemented on the ground. If I look at my own experience, very rarely if there was a request by the Commander of the Republic's headquarters, the police units very rarely participated in any combat activities, even though the police in Sarajevo was the first one to be exposed to the aggression. Also, unfortunately, the HVO's participation, together with the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the ground, did not happen always. My own, for instance, experience is that there was an attempt to break the siege of Sarajevo in June of 1992. I even had an opportunity to announce on Radio Sarajevo that some of the Territorial Defence units of peasants, together with the HVO, were coming through Kiseljak to Ilidza. However, very shortly following this information we received information that in Kiseljak they did not get permission from the HVO to pass through and so this first attempt to break the siege fell through. Also one of the first targets of the aggression was the telecommunications system. I just want to point this out because it was not possible to use the electronics communications to pass information in a timely fashion to the subordinate staffs. It happened that certain information or certain orders would take several days to get through via messengers.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, as part of problems on the ground, including communication problems that you have just mentioned, is it the case that sometimes municipalities operated more independently of Sarajevo? For instance, do you know whether or not on some occasions the War Presidency appointed persons to military positions, such as TO Commanders, without the authorisation or appointment from main headquarters in Sarajevo or the Presidency in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not have any personal experience, but in principle, given the fact that there were two parallel chains of command, the Presidency and the War Presidencies in the municipalities, and then there was the military structure, it was -- it could not happen that somebody would be appointed but that it would not be known to the Commander of the headquarters. I will try to explain this. There were daily reports submitted to the Commander of the Territorial Defence and later to the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In other words, there is the Supreme Command and there is a Supreme Commander, which consisted of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Minister of Defence, the Minister of the Interior, and some other individuals who had the authority to organise and conduct affairs of Bosnia-Herzegovina. At first it was the Crisis Presidency then the War Presidency in the municipalities, comprised of a combination of the military and the civilian authorities. They could make proposals to the Presidency, and since the Commander daily reported to the Supreme Commander, they could decide whether somebody could get appointed or not. And now these are my own views: I think that a significant role in the establishment of the command staff or proposals for the appointments of command staff was also played by the SDA Party, and this is with respect to the Bosniak staff members. It took into account the results that certain individuals achieved in the defence of a certain part, area, or even of Bosnia-Herzegovina. But I have no information that anybody would appoint local Commanders and that the Supreme Commander and the Supreme Command of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was not consulted on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, was there a time in 1992 when you went to Konjic, the municipality of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I happened to be there on 17th October, 1992, first in the municipality of Jablanica and on that same day in the Konjic municipality. I must explain how I happened to be there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, can I go backwards, before you get to the part about why you were there? Is it correct that the first time you were in Konjic since the war started was on 17th October, 1992? In other words, you had not been there prior to that time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had not been there prior to that date. I repeat, it was the 17th of October, in the afternoon, around 6 pm, I was in the territory of Konjic municipality. The 17th October, 1992, for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Referring to that time, before you arrived in Konjic, and I am specifically referring to the period between April and October 16th, am I correct that you do not know how the situation in Konjic was on the ground, including how the forces in Konjic were working?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not know anything, for the simple reason that within the framework of the headquarters of the BiH army there were specific competencies of people, and bodies whose task it was to monitor the situation throughout the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In view of the fact that at the time I was Deputy Commander of the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, my principal duties were focused on Sarajevo and the surroundings. The information that we received from the ground was concentrated in the operational department and at briefings the Commander was informed about them. I had no information from that period which was significant for myself in view of my position.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Is it correct, then, sir, that for instance you would not know who the various TO Commanders in Konjic were, for the period before you got to Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know, but I tried to explain that at the time my scope of activity was not at the level of municipal staffs but it was at a higher level.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Just for an overview, sir -- I am going to go back in a minute and ask you about your time in Konjic, but, just for an overview, can you say how long it was that you remained in the Konjic area, after the 17th October?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Counting the little free time I had -- I am joking, I spent 40 days there, plus for 28 days my people in the army protected me, so that somebody would not kill me, so that in all I spent 42 days in the territory of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you please tell us why in October you were sent to Konjic and what your duties and responsibilities were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In view of the fact that we were not satisfied with the way in which defence was being carried out in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Presidency decided to relocate the main headquarters of the BiH army to the area of Igman. This meant that the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command, together with several of his assistants, needed to be in command of the armed struggle from the area of Igman, an area that was free and under the control of the BiH army. In view of the fact that at the time I was a member of a delegation of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina at a session of the United Nations in September, 1992, and that I took advantage of the opportunity to convey at both a press conference and in contact with people from the American military establishment, the facts about what was happening in Bosnia-Herzegovina, about the aggression committed, about the genocide of the Bosniak people, as well as the Serbs and Croats who do not support the SDS or HDZ policies, and that as a representative of the Supreme Command, I was a Serb, it was necessary, upon my return, for us to meet at Igman with the Chief of Staff of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So that, out of incomprehensible reasons, I had to take a taxi to get through so that allegedly I should not be caught by someone, and thus I reached Konjic, intending to provide accommodation and the necessary resources for pulling out the Chief of Staff of the headquarters, and at the same time to gain insight into the operational situation and to brief the Chief of Staff about it once he was pulled out of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Before you went to Konjic did you know Mr. Zejnil Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: When you went to Konjic did you have occasion to meet him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean before?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: No, I am sorry, sir, when you went to Konjic, in the period from October 17th forward, did you ever meet Zejnil Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I met him for about 10 times.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And during the time you were in Konjic, what position did Mr. Delalic hold?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For me at the time he was Commander of Tactical Group 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And do you know who appointed him to the position of Tactical Group 2?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A moment ago, when I said that for me he was Commander of Tactical Group 2, until that moment and until he introduced himself to me I was not aware of this appointment. I think I did not see the document to that effect, but he, I think he was appointed by the Commander or the Chief of Staff, because according to the principle I referred to a moment ago it should have been the President of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. But I did say that under certain conditions the President of the Presidency could transfer some of his powers directly to the Chief of Staff of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And who was the Chief of Staff of the Bosnian army at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, sir, if I understood you correctly, you said Mr. Delalic was head of Tactical Group 2. Do you remember the number of the Tactical Group that Mr. Delalic was in charge of, and in particular, do you know whether -- who would have been the head of Tactical Group 1, and could that have been Mr. Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise, I did not --

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The answer was he was Commander of Tactical Group 2; she cannot now lead him into a totally different answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may, your Honour, I did not understand a part of your question, whether you asked me whether there were several Groups. Is that your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am asking you, sir, whether you are sure the number of the Tactical Group Mr. Delalic was in charge of was number 2, or could it also have been another number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said Tactical Group 2; however, what I do not know is the composition of the units belonging to his Tactical Group 2. If I may be allowed to say, a Tactical Group is, according to the theory of tactics, a provisional formation which comprises a varying number of units of different organisational structure and composition. It is the size of a strengthened battalion, roughly, which may contain, in addition to infantry units, artillery, armoured units, engineering units, signals units and so on. I did not enter into the composition of that group and am not aware of the strength of the forces under his command.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was being head of a Tactical Group a senior position within the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can say that as these are temporary formations, command over a Tactical Group could be entrusted to an officer of different rank, because a Tactical Group is formed for a particular mission, for a particular time, and upon the completion of the mission it is abolished. Since we are talking about a battalion, a strengthened battalion in terms of size, the practice in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina differed from theory. At the time, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina did not have ranks. The people who came from the former Yugoslav People's Army, though most of us renounced those ranks, we were addressed by the ranks that we had in that army. However, the rest were addressed according to the positions they held, so that they were referred to as "Commander", "Leader", "Chief of Staff"; and I think that at that time Zejnil Delalic did not have any rank. As for what rank a Commander of a Tactical Group may have, let me convey an experience I had in Sarajevo, which may be of assistance. It could happen in Sarajevo for a Brigade Commander to have the rank of Brigadier and another one to have the rank of Major, so that to say what rank the Commander of Tactical Group 1 would have, that depended. If at that time he had the rank of Colonel he would be Colonel, or if he had the rank of Captain, he would be a Captain. There were no ranks at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you know who Mr. Delalic's superior was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to this system of command and control, as the Commander of Tactical Group 1, his superior would have to be the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, can you just indicate, do you know whether Mr. Delalic was head of Tactical Group 1 or Tactical Group 2? I am not sure if I have --

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: With respect, that question has been asked twice. She is desperately trying to get the different answer. She cannot cross-examine her own witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If I may respond. In his answer the witness has stated Mr. Delalic was head of Tactical Group 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You can leave this, if it is necessary for re-examination. Leave it for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Fine, your Honour. Sir, can you -- do you recall where and when you met Mr. Delalic for the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 17th October I was in his house to deal with the problem of one of the undisciplined Commanders of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Juka Prazina.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you describe in some more detail the first occasion when you met Mr. Delalic and what happened during that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I was brought from Croatia to Bosnia-Herzegovina in a manner that was inappropriate, in my view -- when I use this term I am referring to the fact that I was Deputy Commander, or rather Deputy Chief of Staff of the main command of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that the people who should have respected this fact did nothing for a man with such a position. To reach Igman, as had been agreed, when I left Sarajevo on 20th September, 1992, I have already told you that I was transported by taxi, along round about routes via Posusje to Jablanica. When I was talking to the Commander of the Jablanica Territorial Defence, I was called up from Konjic, where I was told I should report urgently because of problems that have cropped up at that very moment. I did not know what it was about. I was driven to the building where Delalic was and several men, among whom I recognised two. The one I knew was Mr. Juka Prazina, who was at the time Commander of a Special Brigade of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and there was also Dragan Andric. I know Dragan Andric from before the war. Delalic I met for the first time then. He surprised me by his strength and size, because at the time much was going on in Bosnia-Herzegovina and there were few people who were in such good physical shape. He showed me a document in which the Chief of Staff of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina gave instructions to investigate the case of the Commander of the Special Brigade of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time. Actually, Juka Prazina came to Igman for the first time on 15th October. He entered the command, the headquarters of one of our units. He physically assaulted the members of the staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Are you requesting these details?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, if I may, let me direct me a little bit more narrowly, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Is it the case that when you met Mr. Delalic he gave you a briefing on the situation of Konjic, or asked someone to do so on his behalf?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will tell you about that later. He did not on that -- at that point of time, because I had come there to deal with a specific problem, without previously being informed of what was happening in Konjic. Allow me to say two more sentences only. So the Chief of Staff had given instructions to deal with the problem of Juka. What was necessary was to interrogate all the people who had been eyewitnesses of that incident, and our decision was that he should be temporarily detained, so as to establish the facts of the matter, as to what had happened in Igman. But that is not essential for this, so I will go on. The next day, on the 18th, Mr. Delalic called Dragan Andric, who was an operative officer in the staff of the Territorial Defence of Konjic, and asked him to brief me on the military situation in the area of Konjic. It was then that I was informed about facts that were relevant for the military situation. Briefly, you know very well that there is a certain order of information, the deployment of the aggressor or enemy forces, the deployment of our own forces, of the units of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the MUP, the HVO, all the units that were stationed in that area. He informed me of the decision of the headquarters regarding the defence of Konjic, and he presented the problems that existed in Konjic at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, during the time that you were in Konjic did you ever see Mr. Delalic meeting with other representatives from the Supreme Command from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This was later, somewhere around the beginning of November. While I was there, I do not know about the situation before, people from the Supreme Command of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina would come there and their task was to prepare the lifting of the blockade of Sarajevo. At that time, as representatives of the Supreme Command, there was Mr. Vehbija Karic, Alija Ismet, Mirsad Causevic, and many others who passed through Konjic on their way to other assignments. However, I was not present if there were any meetings or discussions with those people.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Do you know whether or not Mr. Delalic ever made any written reports to the headquarters, written or oral reports to headquarters in Sarajevo, concerning the situation in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know whether he was in regular contact with the headquarters, and it would have been normal for him to do so as Commander of a Tactical Group. I know that once he showed me a report relating to the situation that had set in because of the operations of the HVO in the area of Prozor. It was a dramatic situation in which it could have been seen from the report he requested assistance to deal with the problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, can I just clarify, was this report to the Supreme -- to the headquarters in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was prepared, and how it was transmitted to the headquarters, I do not know, but I know that it had been prepared for sending. The main problem was that on the 18th and 19th the relations between the HVO and the citizens, the Bosniaks of Prozor, were aggravated and on the night between the 23rd and the 24th a military formation of the HVO appeared. We later assessed that they belonged to the Croatian army. They appeared together with tanks, and the Commander of that armoured unit was Smidt.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, I think it might be more helpful for the judges if I try to, sir, just direct your questions. At the end if you think there has not been enough of an explanation you can inform me of that. Let me just then sir, if I may, ask you: during the problems in Prozor that you have mentioned was there ever a time when someone from the municipal headquarters of Prozor reported to Mr. Delalic about these problems?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not familiar with any report, but the Commander of the municipal headquarters of Prozor, I think Mr. Sabic or Sadic, did come, and he -- I happened to be present. He briefed us on what was happening to the Bosniaks in Prozor, in dramatic terms. According to his report, on --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am not going to ask you at this point about the details of what was going on in Prozor. Let me ask you: was there an occasion later when you and Mr. Delalic were interviewed by TV journalists, where the problems in Prozor were discussed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know about the details, but I did grant an interview for the simple reason that the public of Bosnia-Herzegovina needed to be informed about what was happening in that area, and it had to do with HVO operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was Mr. Delalic also interviewed at the same time, as part of the same programme?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he was, but I am not quite sure. If you have the recording, I think that Karic was there as well when we were interviewed. I know that the journalists -- the reporter was Maric. Maybe he can testify about it. I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Later on I will be asking you to view an excerpt of a video. For now, let me stay with Konjic itself, sir. During the time you were in Konjic did you ever go to any military warehouse to view supplies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but not only military warehouses. I was interested in the overall situation regarding defence, so rather what were the chances, what were the military chances for the units of Jablanica, Konjic and Mostar to assist in the lifting of the blockade of Sarajevo. I toured the military warehouses and established the situation with respect to armaments and material. I was disappointed, because I believe that there was sufficient equipment in those warehouses to undertake something significant.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, let me direct you more specifically. Did you ever go to any warehouse that was located in the Celebici facilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is a military warehouse, as I see something like it here. I think it is this building over here that is marked H, I think. (Indicates). I think that could be it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, whose warehouse was this? Who controlled it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I knew, it was under the control of Tactical Group 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And who brought you to this warehouse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Commander of Tactical Group 2, no one else could -- or more specifically, Mr. Delalic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: When you were there, did you visit the facilities within Celebici where the prisoners were kept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know that there were any such facilities in Celebici. I did not visit them. My aim was to see the warehouse. Whether they were there and where, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, you have talked before about your understanding of a Tactical Group. Who determined, sir, the parameters of the authority of a particular Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The main staff of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, is it correct that a Tactical Group could have authority only over certain units assigned to that Group? Is it also true that a Tactical Group could also have territorial responsibility, meaning authority over geographic area, including all the units in that territorial area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only what was assigned to him under his command by the main headquarters. Only those units were subordinated to him, and no others in principle or in theory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Ms. McHenry, we might have to break here and reassemble at 12.00. The Trial Chamber will now rise. (11.30 am) (Short break) (12.00 pm) (Witness enters court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Will you kindly remind the witness that he is still on his oath?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I am reminding you, sir, that you are still testifying under oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Ms. McHenry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Thank you, sir. Sir, within a Tactical Group who was responsible for maintaining the order and discipline among the units and soldiers that are part of the Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me, there is no feed to the booth. There is no sound.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am sorry, I think there is some problem with this.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, the interpreter is saying there is no sound feeding into the English booth. I see that the microphones are on, but there is no feed into the booth.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: There is a problem with the technical equipment. Can you say one, two, three, four into the microphone?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Still there is no feed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Check with the technicians whether they can come or not. Let the technicians come and check it. (Pause). Okay, we will rise for 10 minutes so that they will come to check it. (12.05 pm) (Short break) (12.15 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We have come to an arrangement whereby we continue to about 1.15 instead of 1.00 and then, still not cheating ourselves, return by 2.45. Therefore we are still not losing the time. (Witness enters court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Are you comfortable now? You may proceed, Ms. McHenry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, I understand that the technical problems have been fixed, and although you answered my previous question, because your answer was not in interpreted let me ask it again, please. Sir, who was responsible for maintaining order and discipline among the units and soldiers who were part of a Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the overall situation, it was the Commander of the Tactical Group. But at a level of each unit it would be the Commander of the unit, at platoon level the Commander of the platoon, at the company level the Commander of the company, and they were subordinate to the Commander of the Tactical Group. So it is through these subordinate commanders that the Commander of the Tactical Group maintained the order and the Commanders of the units were subordinate to the Tactical Group Commander, and because directly the Tactical Group Commander has no particular responsibility to any single individual soldier.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And, sir, who was responsible for ensuring that a reporting system, or a system for transmitting information, existed from the intermediate command levels to the head of a Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Within a system of command one of the elements is reporting; that is, the subordinate Commanders are -- had a duty to report to the Commander in the morning, if this is a combat assignment or if there is anything pressing, so the Commanders of the subordinate units are reporting to the Commander of the Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, you indicated previously that the authority of a Tactical Group Commander would depend on what was assigned to him under his command by the main headquarters. With the Registrar's assistance, I would like to have you look at two documents, Prosecution Exhibit 99-7 annex 9 and Prosecution Exhibit 99-7 annex 7. We have extra copies for the judges. These documents are already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder if the Prosecutor also has extra copies for Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Defence counsel, have you been given them? I think there were extra copies there for Defence counsel. May I just clarify with the usher that both annex 7 and annex 9 have been given to the witness, two different annexes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, 9 and 7.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to direct your attention first to the document dated 11th July, which is annex 9, and --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, can I also get a copy of the document in Bosnian, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to direct your attention to annex 9, which is the document dated July 11th. Can you please indicate what this document indicates as the authority given to Mr. Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My interpretation is that this document appoints Mr. Zejnil Delalic to the Commander of the Tactical Group. I do not know, it states Tactical Group 1. I do not know if that is a typo or something, but it is not clear what units are enter, are part of this Tactical Group. Here it refers to the areas of Hadzici, Konjic and Jablanica, and that would imply that the units from those areas would comprise this Tactical Group. It cannot be gleaned from the document which units these are, but as Commander, Zejnil Delalic had to have known which units comprised this Tactical Group. I do not see such a document stating that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, going forward now to the document dated 27th July, which is annex 7, can you indicate, does this document state what the responsibility of Mr. Delalic is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is similarly as with the previous document. It is not clear what units are -- that comprise this Tactical Group that is responsible for the area of Dreznica, Jablanica, Prozor, Konjic, Pazaric, Hadzici and Igman. This is a good example of what I have already tried to point out to the Trial Chamber. As I repeat, the law of defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina provides that the armed forces consist of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the HVO, the units of the Ministry of the Interior, or as we used to call them, the police, and the units of the organisations within the companies or state institutions. So, from this -- from this document, I cannot see what formations are included, so the document is not precise, and it is not -- does not fall within the framework of the documents that were produced for the combat operations. So, what it says also is that the previous appointments for this area are null and void. Because this is not an order, this is just an appointment of Zejnil Delalic to the post of Commander, but it does not specify which formations, which units are under his -- are being put under his command.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Does the document say anything about what formations are put -- in particular, let me ask you what "Svih" -- can you please indicate what the document says about what formations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Neither of these two documents does not specify any of the particular units in the areas of Pazaric, Hadzici, so from neither of the two documents is it clear which are the units that are under Mr. Delalic's command. And had it been done then, at the time, it would have been very good if all the formations that were targeted to be a part of the armed forces were in reality part of them. Here I speak not for the region of Konjic but the entire Bosnia-Herzegovina. I am trying to say that it is, should also be specified which units are put under a particular Commander's command.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: According to this document, what does when the document says-- first of all, let me ask you, directing your attention to the first line of paragraph 1, when it says "Svih", what does "Svih" mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would mean that you take the law of the defence and read, and in there you read "all", all, all. But the Commander did not order that the HVO, the police, all units of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina be included. So that is just a general term, "all", but in the military documents it has to be specified. All units have to be specified, because it is not the authority, or it is not the responsibility of the Commander in question to specify the units. So he is not responsible for ordering these municipal -- so it is not his responsibility to order any particular unit to be put under his command unless it was specified by the Supreme Commander of the main headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Sir, am I correct that in traditional military structures the individual units are part of larger entities such as battalions or Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. The basic tactical unit is the battalion, and the first joint unit is a brigade. During my time this was the period when the brigades and Corps were being established, and in the area of Sarajevo the brigades had already been formed, as well as the Sarajevo Corp.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you know, at this time -- excuse me one minute. And do you know, at this time in Konjic had brigades and Corps already been formed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the Corps was not, but the brigades were in the process of being formed, because one of my main tasks which I received on 2nd November, 1992, from the Supreme Command, was to assist in forming of the brigades in Neretvica and Jablanica. At that time, the Konjic Brigade was in the process of being formed, but the formation was not completed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did the fact that these larger entities did not then exist create certain problems in using and co-ordinating and controlling the actions of the different municipalities for the task?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The question is not entirely clear to me, but I will try to answer it to the extent that I have understood it. There was a certain latitude in decision-making within the overall task that the headquarters of the municipal headquarters received from the superiors. The orders that were received by the Commander of the Tactical Group, which is not clear here, since the basic task of these units at the time when I was in Konjic was the preparation for the lifting of the blockade of Sarajevo, all headquarters and the Tactical Group were working on the preparations, which included preparing the equipment and staffing for the lifting of the blockade. There was latitude within the scope of preparations, and so the mode of preparation, on the part of the Commanders of a Tactical Group, but not in terms of the timing and preparing and bringing the required troops for the execution of the task.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, do you know when the Tactical Group headed by Mr. Delalic was disbanded? Even if you do not know the exact date, can you give the approximate date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not know the date even approximately. The last time I saw the gentleman was November 23rd, and later activities in the area of Konjic I was not familiar with, because I was cut off, as I said, and as my friends Croats would say, I was arrested by a unit in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, before your arrest, during the time you were still in Konjic in November, did the Tactical Group, to your knowledge, headed by Mr. Delalic, still exist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, you have previously testified concerning your contacts with Mr. Delalic during this time and I am specifically referring to your testimony that the Commander of the Prozor headquarters came to Konjic to brief Mr. Delalic concerning the problems in Prozor. Sir, my question is: was this behaviour consistent or inconsistent with Mr. Delalic having authority over the municipal headquarters of Prozor?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have an objection. The witness did not say that the Commander of the Prozor headquarters came to inform Zejnil Delalic, he just said that the Commander of the TO Prozor came to report about the events, but not to report to Zejnil Delalic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let me clarify, if I have misunderstood or mischaracterised. Sir, let me go back for a minute. Do you know why the Commander of the Prozor headquarters came to Konjic when you previously -- when you were testifying about that? In other words, what was he doing when he went there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Commander of the municipal headquarters of the armed forces of Prozor, in my assessment, abandoned his unit, not to use a more explicit term, came to Konjic to report on what had happened in Prozor in the period from roughly 18th or 19th until he reached us on the 25th of October, 1992. He reported to Karic, who then came as a representative of the main staff of the armed forces to Konjic, and I mentioned some other people. I was present and General Delalic was present when he informed us about the way in which the HVO had acted, as well as units of the Croatian army, whose Commander of armoured forces was Smidt.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, let me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, let us get this clear. Who was he reporting to when he came there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was reporting to representatives of the main staff of the armed forces, and also present was the Commander of Tactical Group 2, Zejnil Delalic. So on behalf of the main staff it was Mr. Karic and myself and Zejnil Delalic. So it was not to Zejnil Delalic as the Commander, but to Zejnil Delalic who was Commander of a Tactical Group in that area, a group which was the best organised as a unit in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Sir, I am going to ask you to view an excerpt from a videotape and ask you if you recognise this as an excerpt of the interview given by you and Mr. Delalic. I would ask the technical people that the excerpt from I25, which is marked as Prosecution Exhibit 115, be shown. After it is shown, I will have a question for you. (Interview played)

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: (translating video). "Mr. Delalic, these conflicts also occurred in the municipalities which are in your zone of responsibility. Mr. Karic just said he was an optimist and that a number of things have been agreed on, in other words that good progress has been made. Could you briefly tell us whether the things that have been agreed and decided upon are being implemented? "Answer: This is still quite fresh. We only sat down together several days ago, but today is the day when we are beginning to see the first results. There is a feeling in the population, among the soldiers of both of these formations, a spirit of friendship, a lessening of tensions which have existed for months. We are in a broad area between what until very recently was still called rather unclearly the new state or province of Herceg Bosna and pure Bosnia, so to speak, so that on both sides we were often the black sheep. "Obviously, because the politicians had not worked out certain things in a timely fashion, and which the military has now, how shall I put it, tackled it in a more serious and active way, and I believe has been very successful in resolving them. The positions are being mixed again. The soldiers of the HVO formations and our units are meeting again as they did previously. We witnessed them kissing and embracing and so forth. Suddenly, it has been understood that this is a very clear struggle against a very clear and specific enemy."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask you, when the interviewer reported that the problems in this area were within the municipalities which were within Mr. Delalic's zone of responsibility, is that an indication, sir, that Mr. Delalic had territorial authority over certain areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From this clip of his interview, that cannot be seen, nor did he have authority in that area. What Mr. Zejnil Delalic is referring to was 10 or 12 days after the attack by the HVO and the Croatian army on Prozor. He is speaking about the settling down of the situation when a joint commission was formed on 26th or the 27th October, in which, as far as I can remember, Mr. Pasalic, Mr. Karic and, on the part of the Croatian army, or rather the HVO, Mr. Kalik were members. With their appearance in Prozor and the tour of the units of the HVO, and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the situation calmed down. That is how I interpret this statement by Mr. Delalic. One cannot see from this, nor did he have authority at the time over the municipal staffs of the armed forces of Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And sir, how do you interpret, let me move forward with another question and I would like to ask you to show a document, Prosecution Exhibit 189.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I can just add that I remember that this interview took place between the 29th October and the 1st or 2nd November, so that the situation was quite different from the one we were discussing, that is the situation in Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, am I correct that this document orders municipal staff of the Bosnian armed forces of Prozor to withdraw all units from their current position and form a line of defence in another position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what it says in the order, to withdraw the armed forces of the Prozor municipal staff to a new line of defence immediately below the town. Whether this was under instructions from the superior -- that means the Commander -- of the Chief of Staff of the main headquarters, I am not -- I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, does this document give any indication whether or not from some source Mr. Delalic has been given authority over the Prozor municipal staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One could make the conclusion that he was given a task on the basis of consultations with the Supreme Commander of the armed forces, that is the Chief of Staff of the main staff of the armed forces, as is stated in the preamble. The way in which it is written, he was authorised by the Chief of Staff of the armed forces to assist in dealing with the problems that had arisen in relations with the HVO on the 27th August, 1992. So it can be concluded from this that he had consultations with the headquarters in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, is this document consistent or inconsistent with the 27th July order, stating that Mr. Delalic has authority over all units, all of the Bosnian army in areas which include Prozor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. I think that this -- by this order the Chief of Staff of the main headquarters is trying to clearly define the area of responsibility and the forces that could be, at a given moment, under the command of the Commander of the Tactical Group, because if I may refer to my analysis of the 27th July, I said that it was not indicated which unit Zejnil Delalic could command. This is a specific assignment that can be given for a particular time period.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, I would like you, now, to look at Prosecution Exhibit 99-7 annex 10, which is also previously in evidence. We have extra copies for your Honours, and if Defence counsel do not have their prior copies, we have extra copies for Defence counsel. Sir, I would like to specifically direct your attention to the paragraphs, at the present time, 4 and 5 of this document, and, sir, am I correct that this document orders the municipal command of the Bosnia-Herzegovina armed forces in Konjic, it orders the municipal headquarters and the Konjic military police to introduce a duty roster, and it orders an offensive to be launched?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may be permitted, I should first like to mention, again, the preamble, which says, "pursuant to the orders of the Supreme Command of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina", which means that again he received an order, and we do not know what that order is from this document, and he is then ordering the command of the municipal command of the armed forces of Konjic to regulate these things as you have said, that the military police should introduce the duty roster and the next thing that you said. So, the Supreme Command has transferred to him, because you see some expressions are being used which show that they did not reach the subordinated staffs, because this was the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command, not the Supreme Commander, and that an offensive be launched immediately using forces deployed in Bjelimici against Kalinovik. I do not know as to the Operation Jug or South at the time, but he is probably ordering those units in the Konjic municipal staff, which are not within a part of his Tactical Group. If I may ask your Honours, I notice that I made a slip in using Tactical Group 1 and Tactical Group 2; as you yourself noticed, I said Tactical Group 2. So in effect it is Tactical Group 1, and this document shows that it was preceded by an order received from a superior and that superior is also the Chief of Staff of the armed forces, that is Mr. Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Does this document indicate that at some point Mr. Delalic was given authority over the Konjic municipal headquarters, and is this document consistent or inconsistent with the authority given Mr. Delalic over all formations in the 27th July document, for an area including Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am reading the order to mean that he was given a specific task, not that it shows that he is the Commander of all the armed forces. He is being given a specific assignment, as we have already indicated. But this document is addressed to the War Presidency of Konjic, more as a report than as an order. So it may be a little confusing that he is extending his authority. I do not see from this document that his authority, defined in previous documents, has been expanded, but they are only expressed in specific terms. I apologise, we saw that a moment ago linked with the order for Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, at this time now I would be turning -- I may return back later to this document, but for now I would be turning to -- excuse me, excuse me, your Honour, I forgot your prior direction, excuse me. Sir, let me turn now to a different area. Previously there was a discussion of Celebici. Could you please report when the first time you learned that there was a prison in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At a briefing on 18th October, 1992, when there was a briefing on the general situation in Konjic. It was stated that there were two prisons in which the people who participated in the attack on Konjic were being detained, that is military personnel. So that was within the framework of a briefing. It was said that these facilities existed in Celebici, and I think a sports hall in Konjic, somewhere in the old town.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: During your time in Konjic did you come to learn who the Commander of this prison was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At one point, while I was in the premises where the municipal staff of the armed forces of Konjic was housed, because that is where my premises were also, at the end of October, I was told who the Commander was, and shown -- that was once, and I saw him once again later, but nothing special -- there was nothing special about it which would attract my attention to the Commander of the military prison in Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the person you learned was the Commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Five or six years later, if you are thinking of Mr. Mucic, if that was what he was at the time. I think so, but I cannot be very definite. One forgets names, they fade out.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you have any dealings with or any conversation with the camp commander concerning the prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you ever see the camp commander and Mr. Delalic together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not together, not together, but I said that I saw the gentleman where his place was, that is within the staff that was in control of him and the prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And where was this place that you have referred to, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is in Konjic, the motel which was used by the municipal staff and its bodies and where I had my office, and where I spent my time while I stayed in Konjic. I spent part of the time there and part of the time in a military facility in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, during the time that you were in Konjic, did Mr. Delalic ever say anything to you about Celebici, the prison in particular?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not discuss that subject in particular, but on one occasion, this must have been somewhere in mid November, he was talking about problems in general that he was having as a Commander, for the simple reason that relations were worsening with representatives of the Croatian people. He spoke about threats that he had been subjected to, and on that occasion he mentioned a detail, that is an attempt, and I remembered the name. This may be because the same man had pointed a pistol at me, that is Mitke Pirkic, who had tried to enter the prison by force, and said that he was simply worried that someone might place in jeopardy the persons who were being interrogated. That is all that -- all the discussion that the two of us had linked to the military prison in Celebici. But if I may convey some more observations of mine, something that I learned touring the units and talking to the soldiers. Several soldiers expressed their dissatisfaction with the fact that those who were in prison had three meals a day, whereas the soldiers who were defending Konjic received food only twice. This surprised me a little, not this difference between two and three meals, but why they were telling me about it, and I realised that in a situation in which they were short of weapons and ammunition and spending 40 hours and more on the front-lines, continuously, they responded perhaps with some insufficient control, saying why people who had participated in the attack on the town should be treated in such a way, whereas the troops who were risking their own lives had such poor conditions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: During the time you were in Konjic, do you know if the Red Cross visited Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not familiar with the details, but one evening I remember coming for a brief visit and since I saw him 12 times, sometimes we had coffee together, and I remember that in front of the facility was a Red Cross team and Zejnil Delalic told me then that they had visited it, that the instructions had come from Sarajevo, and, according to the information conveyed to me by Delalic at the time, they had found the situation to be satisfactory. That must have been between the 2nd or 3rd and the 5th November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, when the Red Cross went into an area, who generally authorised the Red Cross to go to a particular prison? My question is both directed on the Republic level and in the more local level where the prison in question was located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time I was in Konjic, I was not familiar with the system of decision-making, but later on, in 1993/94 and during the time I was assistant commander for co-operation with civilian authorities, I learned about the system, the system of control carried out by the Red Cross. They could go to prisons after receiving permission from the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which transferred its authority in the case of military prisons to the Supreme Command of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina; and the Supreme Command would then give direct orders to subordinate headquarters, if there were any such problems to allow the Red Cross to visit, so that this decision always went from the top down to the subordinate staffs and units.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Showing you an excerpt, sir, from a video. It is Prosecution Exhibit 115, tape I25. I do not believe there is any text on this, it is just a photo, sir. I ask if you can look at that and tell what is being shown. (Video played)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: International Committee of the Red Cross to the Commander, Zejnil Delalic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
